notes:
These notes on 1 Samuel 25:23–44 are drawn only from pages I actually read. A few gaps up front:

- **Catholic and Orthodox:** I found nothing on newadvent.org, catholic.com or oca.org, so there are no notes from those traditions.
- **Prosperity, word-of-faith and hyper-grace teaching:** I found nothing on this passage.
- **Modern scholarship:** I only got a short Bible Odyssey piece.
- **Enduring Word:** the full page cut off partway through Abigail's speech, so most of Guzik's points below come from search snippets and his Blue Letter Bible study guide.
- **Denominational differences:** the real disagreements I found are between individual teachers, not clearly between denominations.

**v. 23**
- Gill says she bowed out of respect for how important David was. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-samuel/25-23.html
- Guzik pictures an angry David stopped in his tracks by a long line of gifts with a beautiful woman bowing at its head. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-25/
- Matthew Henry notes that she took the posture of a penitent and a petitioner, in front of her own servants and David's soldiers, for her household's sake. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-samuel/25-23.html

**v. 24**
- Constable: Nabal had called David a runaway servant, but Abigail humbly calls herself David's servant. Like Christ riding a donkey, she takes the fools' sins on herself. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/1-samuel-25.html
- Guzik: she asks permission to speak rather than taking over the conversation. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/guzik_david/StudyGuide_1Sa/1Sa_25.cfm
- Mary Baxter compares her to Daniel: as Nabal's wife, she counted herself one with him and took his sin on herself. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/baxter_mary/WitW/WitW20_Abigail.cfm

**v. 25**
- Henry: she excuses Nabal by blaming his natural lack of understanding. By saying she never saw the young men, she hints that he usually takes her advice. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-samuel/25-30.html
- Constable asks whether a wife should speak of her husband this way. He suggests she meant Nabal had proved true what others called him. Quoting Levenson, he says she outwardly defends Nabal while quietly separating herself from him. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/1-samuel-25.html
- Precept Austin: she agrees Nabal was wholly wrong but says he isn't worth David's attention. https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-samuel-25-commentary
- Bible Odyssey (modern scholarship): Nabal's name comes from the Hebrew root *nbl*, which is used elsewhere for folly and offensive behaviour. Abigail means "my father's joy." https://www.bibleodyssey.org/articles/abigail/

**v. 26**
- Guzik: she speaks as if David has already turned back, which gently steers him toward that outcome. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-25/
- Ellicott: she treats Nabal as too insignificant to matter, and wishes David's other enemies were just as harmless. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-samuel-25.html

**v. 27**
- Ellicott: "gift" (literally "blessing") was the customary present an inferior brought to a superior, meant for David's men. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-samuel-25.html
- Guzik: her plea worked partly because she paid David what he was owed. By taking it, David accepted that the bill was settled. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-25/

**v. 28**
- Ellicott: she again takes the blame, so David's forgiveness will be shown to her, and this draws out his "chivalry." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-samuel-25.html
- Guzik: although David's anger at the moment was plainly sin, she praises his overall character and treats this as out of character. https://blueletterbible.org/Comm/guzik_david/StudyGuide2017-1Sa/1Sa-25.cfm
- Constable: she believed God would give David a lasting dynasty because he fought the Lord's battles, not just Saul's. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/1-samuel-25.html

**v. 29: the main point of disagreement ("bundle of the living")**
- *Meaning safety in this life:*
  - Keil says the words refer first to God keeping the righteous safe on earth. He adds that God will not let such a person perish even at death. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_samuel/25-29.htm
  - The Cambridge-style note on the same page says the immediate reference is "of course" David's earthly life. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_samuel/25-29.htm
  - Barnes reads the "bundle" as a bag that holds valuables. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_samuel/25-29.htm
- *Meaning eternal life:*
  - Ellicott calls it one of the earliest clear expressions of belief in an eternal future with God. He notes it is a common inscription on Jewish gravestones. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_samuel/25-29.htm
  - Gill and Henry report the Jewish reading about the life to come. Gill adds that David is kept "among other his chosen ones." https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-samuel/25-29.html
  - William Kelly says she sees David held by God "intimately and for ever." https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-samuel/25-29.html
- *Another reading:* the ESV Study Bible note says it may mean "the book of the living" in Psalm 69:28. https://www.blueletterbible.org/esv-study-bible/notes/1sa/chapter-25
- *On the sling:*
  - Barnes says the picture especially suited David, famous for his sling. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_samuel/25-29.htm
  - Constable cites a custom of shepherds carrying two bags, one for food and one for stones. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/1-samuel-25.html
- *An unusual homily:* one Biblical Illustrator sermon uses the phrase to speak of "the divinity of human nature." It also says people can leave the bundle whenever they choose. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tbi/1-samuel-25.html

**vv. 30–31**
- Coffman: killing Nabal, a well-known man of Judah, would have started a blood feud with clans David would need on his way to the throne. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-samuel/25-30.html
- One note on BibleHub: as a future judge, David must not be troubled by guilt for doing what he would have to condemn in others. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_samuel/25-29.htm
- *Differing views on "remember your maidservant":*
  - Ellicott calls it "exquisite grace," a request for kindness from his throne later. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-samuel-25.html
  - Guzik says she offered herself for David's future consideration, perhaps inappropriately. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-25/
  - Precept Austin thinks it proved wise once Nabal died. https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-samuel-25-commentary
  - Deffinbaugh doubts she understood all she was saying. He compares it to Joseph's request to Pharaoh's cupbearer in Genesis 40. https://bible.org/seriespage/dear-abby-1-samuel-251-44

**vv. 23–31: whether Abigail was a submissive wife (debated)**
- Guzik: she was not especially submissive to Nabal, perhaps justified because lives were at stake. She models "sweetly speaking submission," as opposed to silent or sharp submission. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-25/
- Deffinbaugh: she was unsubmissive only on the surface. She is truly submissive because she tries to save her husband. https://bible.org/seriespage/dear-abby-1-samuel-251-44
- *Seeing Christ in her:* the Gospel Coalition sees in her a glimpse of Jesus, the Mediator who faced wrath for foolish sinners. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/article/abigail-point-christ/

**vv. 32–34**
- Guzik: David knew God was speaking through her, and was wise enough to take advice from a woman. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-25/
- Constable: God used David's conscience to spare Saul, and here used Abigail to spare Nabal. Wise David listens to a stranger, while foolish Nabal wouldn't listen to his own wife. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/1-samuel-25.html
- Baxter: David recognised her as God's messenger. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/baxter_mary/WitW/WitW20_Abigail.cfm

**v. 35**
- ESV Study Bible note: "Go… in peace" means her household is safe. https://www.blueletterbible.org/esv-study-bible/notes/1sa/chapter-25

**v. 36**
- Constable: Nabal behaves like a king, another parallel with proud Saul. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/1-samuel-25.html
- Guzik: Nabal is a picture of the sinner who ignores God's coming judgment. Simply inviting David to this feast would have saved him. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-25/

**v. 37**
- Constable: there is a wordplay on *nebel* ("wineskin"). With the wine gone, Nabal was nothing. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/1-samuel-25.html
- ESV Study Bible note: possibly a heart attack or a stroke. https://www.blueletterbible.org/esv-study-bible/notes/1sa/chapter-25
- Guzik quotes an older writer: the power of her words came "from the Spirit of God." https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/guzik_david/StudyGuide_1Sa/1Sa_25.cfm

**v. 38: how God "struck" Nabal**
- Gill (labelled Calvinist/Baptist on StudyLight) and Wesley (labelled Arminian) agree: either a further disease, or God increased Nabal's grief and fear until it killed him. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-samuel/25-38.html
- Keil: a second stroke. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_samuel/25-38.htm
- Ellicott: nothing more than natural causes is apparent. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-samuel-25.html
- The Cambridge note disagrees: it was divine judgment even though there were partly natural causes. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_samuel/25-38.htm
- Precept Austin links the verse to Romans 12:17–21 (leave vengeance to God). https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-samuel-25-commentary

**v. 39**
- The Homiletical Commentary: "upheld my cause" is courtroom language. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-samuel/25-38.html
- Constable: David's thanks were fitting because he had left Nabal to God. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/1-samuel-25.html

**vv. 39–42: the marriage (critical views)**
- Constable says it was wrong, since God's will has been monogamy from creation. The same words "sent" and "took" reappear in the Bathsheba story. He thinks Abigail had a choice and shouldn't have agreed. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/1-samuel-25.html
- Guzik instead sees David honouring her request to be remembered. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-25/

**v. 41**
- Precept Austin: she is "doubly humble," offering to wash the feet of David's *servants*. https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-samuel-25-commentary

**v. 42**
- Vannoy: she shared in the kingdom of the Lord's anointed, while Nabal became "an empty wineskin." https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-samuel-25-commentary

**v. 43**
- ESV Study Bible note: Ahinoam was probably married first and was the mother of Amnon. Abigail bore Chileab, also called Daniel. https://www.blueletterbible.org/esv-study-bible/notes/1sa/chapter-25

**v. 44**
- Constable: Saul probably treated David as good as dead, or wanted to cancel his claim as son-in-law. The chapter opens with Samuel's death and closes with the loss of Michal. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/1-samuel-25.html
- Henry: David would have stayed faithful to Michal if she had stayed faithful to him. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/1Sa/1Sa_025.cfm
